results.title: Evaluating Container Security and Reproducibility in Research Software Engineering
results.content: However, research containers often include outdated or unnec-essary packages, introducing significant security vulnerabilities that conflict with reproducibility requirements. We design a reproducibility-aware DevSecOps pipeline that scans, hardens, and tests container images using best practices such as SBOM generation, minimal base images, and DockerSlim optimization. Prominent open-source scanners include Trivy [4], known for its speed and ease of integration into CI/CD pipelines; Anchore Engine [5], which offers centralized inspection and policy-based analysis, including the generation of Software Bills of Materials (SBOMs); and Clair [6], recognized for its thorough static analysis of image layers against multiple vulnerability feeds. However, while these bodies of work address either security or reproducibility, there is a critical gap in systematically evaluating the impact of security hardening measures on the functional reproducibility of scientific workflows .The motivation for our work stems directly from this gap and the pressing need for a systematic, empirical evaluation of container security specifically within research domains. Each container image in our dataset was processed through a multi-stage experimental pipeline, depicted in Figure 1, designed to assess its initial security posture, apply hardening techniques, and subsequently evaluate both the security im-provements and the preservation of functional reproducibility. The pipeline would automatically trigger on code changes or updates to base images, build the container (ideally using multi-stage builds from minimal bases), perform vulnerability scanning, apply automated remediation where possible, re-scan, and execute reproducibility tests. The weekly package update baseline represents current practice in many research environments, while our multi-scanner approach provides enhanced security posture through systematic vulnerability detection and remediation. We have presented a novel reproducibility-aware DevSecOps framework that systematically addresses the critical tension between container security and scientific reproducibility in research environments. The framework’s key innovations include: (1) a multi-scanner vulnerability detection protocol that captures complementary security insights across different tools, (2) structured compara-tive analysis methods for evaluating security improvement approaches against operational baselines, and (3) nuanced reproducibility assessment protocols that account for domain-specific tolerances and acceptable scientific variations. This work contributes to the research software engineering community by providing: (1) a systematic methodology for balancing security and reproducibility concerns, (2) vali-dated protocols for multi-scanner vulnerability assessment, (3) structured approaches for comparative security analysis, and (4) complete open-source implementation of all framework components.

results.title: victoriametrics-vmauth Secure-by-Default Container Image
results.content: Chainguard Containers - victoriametrics-vmauth - overview Last changed 3 days ago Be the first to hear about exciting product updates, critical vulnerability alerts, compare alternative images, and more. For those with access, this container image is available on `cgr.dev`: docker pull cgr.dev/ORGANIZATION/victoriametrics:latest Be sure to replace the `ORGANIZATION` placeholder with the name used for your organization's private repository within the Chainguard Registry. Below are the Helm install commands for each component: ### Install `vmagent` helm install vmagent victoria-metrics-agent --repo \ --set image.repository=cgr.dev/chainguard-private/victoriametrics-vmagent \ ### Install `vmauth` helm install vmauth victoria-metrics-auth --repo \ --set image.repository=cgr.dev/chainguard-private/victoriametrics-vmauth \ Note: You will need to set the config and for sample testing purpose, you can take inspiration from this example: cat <<YAML | kubectl apply -f - image: cgr.dev/chainguard-private/victoriametrics-vmauth:latest - "-auth.config=/config/auth.yml" ### Install `vminsert`, `vmselect`, `vmstorage` helm install vminsert victoria-metrics-cluster --repo \ --set =cgr.dev/chainguard-private/victoriametrics-vminsert \ --set =cgr.dev/chainguard-private/victoriametrics-vmselect \ --set =cgr.dev/chainguard-private/victoriametrics-vmstorage \ Note: We use `=""` because our images are alredy coming with `cluster` suffix, so we no longer need to specify it. url: "your PROMETHEUS HTTP API server here" repository: cgr.dev/chainguard-private/victoriametrics-vmalert summary: "{{ $labels.job }} instance: {{$labels.instance }} is not up" description: "Job {{ $labels.job }} instance: {{$labels.instance }} is not up for the last 1 minute" helm install vmalert victoria-metrics-alert --namespace victoriametrics \ helm install vminsert victoria-metrics-cluster --repo \ --set =cgr.dev/chainguard-private/victoriametrics-vmalert \ Chainguard Containers are minimal container images that are secure by default. The main features of Chainguard Containers include: * Minimal design, without unnecessary software bloat * Daily builds to ensure container images are up-to-date with available security patches * High quality build-time SBOMs attesting to the provenance of all artifacts within the image * Verifiable signatures provided by Sigstore * Reproducible builds with Cosign and apko (read more about reproducibility) For cases where you need container images with shells and package managers to build or debug, most Chainguard Containers come paired with a `-dev` variant.
